{"id": "2:283/q01", "question": "What does safar mean and evoke?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q01/p1", "position": "Travel, whose root conveys uncovering or disclosure.", "reasons": "Wahidi cites travel exposing character, the book making clear, dawn, uncovering a face, reconciliation, sweeping, and Ibn al-Aʿrabi's al-Akhtal line; al-Azhari says the traveler emerges into open country and cites daylight and Sirius; Razi repeats these cognates."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q02", "question": "How does 'on a journey' work in the sentence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q02/p1", "position": "It means being in the state of travel; ʿalā evokes firm establishment in it.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan glosses the phrase 'while traveling'; Alusi calls it a dependent metaphor and allows coordination or a circumstantial reading."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q03", "question": "Why mention travel here?", "turns_on": "Whether the conditional describes a typical obstacle or limits lawful pledging.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q03/p1", "position": "Travel is the common setting where writing or witnesses are unavailable; comparable obstacles also call for security.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Elmalılı and Ibn Ashur cite scarcity of scribes, tools, witnesses, night, busyness, or doubtful debtor standing. Burhan notes a conditional need not be legally restrictive. Razi compares the fear clause in 4:101. Jishumi names the common travel shortage of writing and witnesses; Burhan explicitly rejects using this typical shortage to restrict pledges to travel and calls a travel pledge recommended when trustworthy scribes and witnesses are lacking."}, {"id": "2:283/q03/p2", "position": "The travel condition is restrictive for pledges.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Dahhak and Dawud follow the apparent conditional wording; Dahhak also requires absence of a scribe. Tabari rejects its restriction on pledges by the armor report, while others reject it as customary context. Jishumi reports Mujahid's combined travel and no-scribe condition."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q04", "question": "What is read and meant by 'a scribe'?", "turns_on": "Whether the absent resource is a writer, writing materials, or written documents, and how the consonantal text is read.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q04/p1", "position": "Kitāban, writing or writing materials, including pen, ink and paper.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Ubayy, Mujahid and Abu al-Aliya say a writer may be present without materials; Tabari records variant specific lacks of ink, paper, or writer. Nahhas calls it anomalous; Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi find its sense apt despite codex spelling."}, {"id": "2:283/q04/p2", "position": "Kātiban, a single writer.", "reasons": "Tabari prefers the codex and regional reading; Nahhas relates it to 2:282's 'let a writer write'; Thalabi cites the majority and codex. Other sources note the common reading."}, {"id": "2:283/q04/p3", "position": "Kuttāban or kitāban as plural writers.", "reasons": "Dahhak reads a plural of 'writer'; Nahhas says kitāb can be a collective of scribes; Ibn Abbas reasons each case has a scribe."}, {"id": "2:283/q04/p4", "position": "Kutuban, written books or records.", "reasons": "Abu al-Aliya's plural of kitāb fits multiple cases."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q05", "question": "How is 'you do not find a scribe' attached syntactically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q05/p1", "position": "It may coordinate with the condition, attach to kāna's predicate, or be a circumstantial clause.", "reasons": "Samin distinguishes the latter two as nominative-context constructions; Abu Hayyan also lists attachments."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q06", "question": "What is a rahn or pledged security?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q06/p1", "position": "An item retained or delivered as security for a debt; the root also conveys permanence, detention or firmness.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Razi explain transfer from verbal noun to object name; Qurtubi says it is recoverable by sale proceeds. Ibn Ashur adduces 74:38 and Zuhayr; Farisi cites Abu Zayd and 66:12; poetry in Aʿsha and others shows pledged property, persons and enduring food."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q07", "question": "Do rahana and arhana differ in use?", "turns_on": "Whether the two verbs are interchangeable in collateral usage and whether arhana carries a separate bidding sense.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q07/p1", "position": "Both can mean to pledge collateral.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Ibn al-Aʿrabi and al-Akhfash allow both; poetry attributed to Ibn Hammam is adduced, but al-Asmaʿi disputes its wording. Wahidi, Qurtubi, Samin and Tabrisi record the disagreement."}, {"id": "2:283/q07/p2", "position": "Rahana is standard for pledging, while arhana may mean outbidding, giving another's pledge, or keeping something going.", "reasons": "Abu Ali and Abu Zayd distinguish loans and sales from bidding high; Farra gives another-person sense; Ibn Atiyya and Samin cite the high-price camel, and rahantu lisani excludes arhana."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q08", "question": "How is 'pledges' read and formed?", "turns_on": "The transmitted vowels and alif, the regularity of their plural patterns, codex spelling, and usage in horse racing.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q08/p1", "position": "Ruhun, with two dammas and no alif, is a transmitted plural of rahn.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it, with Ibn Abbas, Ubayy's transmission, and others; some analyze it like rare suquf. Zajjaj prefers it for codex fit and valid transmission. Abu Amr distinguishes ordinary pledges from rihān for horse wagers; poetry supports rahn. Nashr assigns the two-ḍamma, no-alif form to Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr."}, {"id": "2:283/q08/p2", "position": "Rihān, with kasra and alif, is the regular plural of rahn.", "reasons": "Most readers use it; Akhfash, Tabari, Nahhas, Razi and Samin favor its productive pattern such as hibal from habl. Sibawayh's caution weighs against invented plurals of plurals; Qiraat-ER also calls it canonical. Nashr specifies kasra on rāʾ, fatḥa on hāʾ and a following alif for the remaining readers."}, {"id": "2:283/q08/p3", "position": "Ruhn, with a still hāʾ, is a lightened form of ruhun.", "reasons": "Reports assign it to Ikrima, Asim, Meccans or particular Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr transmissions; Nahhas explains dropping ḍamma for weight and prefers an adjectival analogy; Akhfash criticizes the rare pattern. Thalabi treats vowelled and unvowelled forms as dialect variants."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q09", "question": "How does 'pledges held' function grammatically?", "turns_on": "The omitted clause element and whether rahn functions as object noun or verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q09/p1", "position": "A nominative subject with omitted predicate, or predicate of an omitted subject such as 'the security'; an implied command to take one is also possible.", "reasons": "Jishumi allows nominative and imperative or accusative ellipses; Razi, Baydawi, Qurtubi's Mahdawi and Samin lay out the alternatives; Alusi treats it as security, a thing to take, or a prescription."}, {"id": "2:283/q09/p2", "position": "The pledge noun is a lexicalized verbal noun used as an object, not a cognate accusative.", "reasons": "Farisi, Wahidi, Razi and Samin distinguish object usage from a verbal noun used adverbially; Ibn Atiyya says its noun status permits the plural with kasra."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q10", "question": "When may a pledge be taken?", "turns_on": "Whether the travel and scribe conditions restrict the law or describe a typical need for security.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q10/p1", "position": "Pledges are valid during travel or residence, with or without an available scribe.", "reasons": "The Prophet pledged armor to a Jewish seller in Medina; reports differ over twenty or thirty measures of barley and the seller's name. Majority jurists treat travel as an example; Razi compares 4:101. Ibn Atiyya says the verse's general meaning itself extends to home. Jishumi reports juristic unanimity against Mujahid's travel restriction; Burhan says the more usual lack of trustworthy scribes and witnesses on journeys explains the wording without limiting the rule."}, {"id": "2:283/q10/p2", "position": "Only during travel, and for some authorities only if a writer is unavailable.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Dahhak and Dawud take the travel and lack-of-scribe conditions literally; Dahhak directs writing instead whenever possible. Jishumi reports Mujahid's requirement of both travel and no available scribe."}, {"id": "2:283/q10/p3", "position": "If writing is available, pledging is permissible but ordinarily not recommended without another reason.", "reasons": "Elmalılı distinguishes legal permission from prudent resort to collateral."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q11", "question": "What does qabḍ mean in 'held in possession'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q11/p1", "position": "Grasping and holding something in the palm.", "reasons": "Jishumi contrasts emphatic ḍād with qabṣ using un-emphatic ṣād, which means holding with the fingertips."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q12", "question": "What does possession do to a pledge's legal effect?", "turns_on": "At what stage the contract binds, and whose physical custody satisfies maqbudah.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q12/p1", "position": "Taking possession is required for validity or binding completion; a mere verbal pledge has no operative security.", "reasons": "Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa treat possession as a condition of validity; many cite 'held.' Jishumi explains that security is incomplete until possession; he contrasts Abu Hanifa's demand for actual possession with Shafi'i's acceptance of legal possession for an undivided share."}, {"id": "2:283/q12/p2", "position": "Malik treats offer and acceptance as a

{"id": "2:283/q14", "question": "What if a pledge returns to the debtor?", "turns_on": "Whether renewed debtor custody undoes the security, and whether its legal form matters.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q14/p1", "position": "Return to the debtor voids the pledge.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya relates this to its defining held state; Qurtubi follows loss of possession. {"id": "2:283/q15", "question": "Can debt claims or uncertain property be pledged?", "turns_on": "Whether the collateral can be physically possessed and realized, especially for debt claims and common shares.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q15/p1", "position": "Only valuable, saleable and deliverable property; debts and uncertain property cannot be pledged.", "reasons": "The majority require realizable security and physical possession. {"id": "2:283/q16", "question": "Can an undivided share be pledged?", "turns_on": "Whether an undivided share can be received as security.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q16/p1", "position": "An undivided share cannot be pledged.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa and the argument cited by Razi and Elmalılı rely on inability to take definite possession. {"id": "2:283/q17", "question": "Which growth of collateral remains pledged?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q17/p1", "position": "The pledged property's inseparable growth follows the pledge, but separable fruits do not unless stipulated.", "reasons": "Qurtubi distinguishes fattening and offspring from crops, milk, wool and fruit, citing independent alms treatment of the latter."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q18", "question": "Does a secured creditor have priority over other creditors?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q18/p1", "position": "The secured creditor has priority over other creditors.", "reasons": "Malik and many jurists give priority when the debtor has not already been declared insolvent; Qurtubi rejects a report of equal sharing."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q19", "question": "May the creditor use pledged property?", "turns_on": "Who owns benefits, who pays upkeep, and whether maintenance or the contract permits creditor use.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q19/p1", "position": "Benefits belong to the owner, who bears upkeep; creditor use requires permission or is forbidden.", "reasons": "A report says the owner gets yield and bears loss. {"id": "2:283/q30", "question": "Who is forbidden to conceal testimony?", "turns_on": "Whether the prohibition directly addresses transaction witnesses alone or also the debtor's acknowledgment.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q30/p1", "position": "Witnesses who know the transaction must disclose their testimony.", "reasons": "Tabari and early authorities address summoned witnesses; Jishumi includes those who attended the contract or pledge without formal appointment. {"id": "2:283/q31", "question": "When must testimony be offered?", "turns_on": "Whether only a formal request triggers the duty, or known danger to a right calls for earlier disclosure.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q31/p1", "position": "When summoned or when a right risks loss, a witness must testify accurately; the duty may arise before being asked.", "reasons": "Tabari, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Atiyya speak of summons and risk; Qurtubi treats testimony as collective duty becoming individual for needed witnesses. {"id": "2:283/q34", "question": "What is the force of 'his heart is sinful'?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase foregrounds a corrupt state of the heart or the sin incurred by this act.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q34/p1", "position": "The concealer's heart becomes guilty, wicked or corrupt; concealment is a grave sin.", "reasons": "Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Suddi and others call the heart wicked. Jishumi calls the concealer's heart disobedient, classifies the act as a major sin, and cites a report comparing the concealer to a false witness."}, {"id": "2:283/q34/p2", "position": "It states the heart has incurred the sin of suppressing testimony.", "reasons": "Mawardi's alternative and Ibn Atiyya stress the guilt attaching to the act. Farisi describes withholding entrusted testimony itself as sin; his accompanying comparison discusses the attachment of 'in sin' in 2:206."}]}
{"id": "2:283/q35", "question": "Why attribute sin to the heart?", "turns_on": "Whether attribution is rhetorical causal language or grounds for a stronger claim that the heart is the acting subject.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q35/p1", "position": "Concealment begins in inward intention and knowledge, and the heart governs outward acts; naming it intensifies blame.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan cite the Prophetic sound-body morsel; Tabrisi cites 58:22; Qurtubi calls it part-for-whole; Ibn Ashur names perception, emotion and intention. Biqai and Bursevi link a corrupted heart to the body. Alusi rejects extra black-mark and body-effect theories. {"id": "2:283/q39", "question": "What does God's knowledge in the close imply?", "turns_on": "Whether the closing universal statement is heard only as warning or also as promise.", "positions": [{"id": "2:283/q39/p1", "position": "God knows hidden and public deeds, including testimony, and will judge and repay them; the close threatens concealment.", "reasons": "Tabari, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Biqai, Ibn Ashur and others draw the warning. {"id": "20:10/q01", "question": "How does the time clause 'when he saw' connect grammatically to the account?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding account has enough event sense to govern idh, or an unspoken command or event must be supplied.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q01/p1", "position": "It modifies the preceding account or report of Moses.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya supplies the implicit action in ḥadīth; al-Ṭabrisī calls it an accusative circumstance; al-Bayḍāwī and Abū Ḥayyān treat the account as an event; al-Sharīf says story and report imply occurrence; al-Ālūsī prefers attachment to the preceding revealed account, since a bare substantive cannot govern the clause."}, {"id": "20:10/q01/p2", "position": "It is the object of an implicit command to remember the time.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ and al-Zamakhsharī are cited for the implied udhkur; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī allow it."}, {"id": "20:10/q01/p3", "position": "It depends on an omitted following event or verb.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī is cited by al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī; al-Nasafī permits an omitted event."}]}
{"id": "20:10/q02", "question": "What journey and circumstances led Moses to see the fire?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in how Moses lost the road and in the journey's particular circumstances.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q02/p1", "position": "Returning from Midian toward Egypt with his family, Moses lost the way on a cold dark night and could not kindle fire.", "reasons": "Muqātil and others specify winter, sometimes Friday, snow, pregnancy or a son's birth, dispersed livestock, no water, and fire to the left or on a mountain near Ṭuwā. {"id": "20:10/q03", "question": "What did Moses actually see when the verse calls it fire?", "turns_on": "Whether 'fire' names a physical fire, divine light perceived as fire, a small visible flame, or an allegorical image; al-Rāzī and Bursevī appeal to prophetic truthfulness.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q03/p1", "position": "He saw divine light that appeared to him to be fire.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī, Ibn ʿAbbās and most exegetes distinguish Moses' perception from God's light; some call it the Lord's light. {"id": "20:10/q04", "question": "What was reported about the tree and fire as Moses approached?", "turns_on": "Reports give different tree species and details of its behavior; al-Rāzī questions whether the Qurʾānic wording establishes any tree.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q04/p1", "position": "The fire appeared in a green tree and did not consume it.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī describes brilliant white fire surrounding the tree from bottom to top without altering its green color; Ibn ʿAbbās marveled at its unchanged beauty.
